meta.title: Best 65-Inch Smart TV Under ₹80,000 in India (2026): Mini LED Picks Ranked
meta.description: Compare the best 65-inch smart TV under ₹80,000 in India for 2026. Mini LED vs QLED panels, 144Hz gaming, Dolby Vision and warranty terms ranked.
meta.short_desc: Mini LED reached ₹80,000 this year. Here is what that actually buys you at 65 inches.

headings.text: What actually matters in a 65-inch TV under ₹80,000

meta.tldr_pick: The Hisense 65E8S is the best 65-inch smart TV under ₹80,000 in India right now. It is a genuine Mini LED panel with local dimming zones, roughly 700 nits of peak brightness, 144Hz VRR gaming support and Dolby Vision plus Dolby Atmos, usually selling in the ₹72,000–₹78,000 window. Verify the exact E8S suffix on the listing before you pay, because Hisense sells lower-tier E7 and A7 models at similar prices.
key_takeaways: Mini LED is genuinely available under ₹80,000 now: the Hisense E8S and TCL Q6C both use real dimming-zone panels, not edge-lit LED with a QLED sticker.
Ignore any brightness claim without a nits figure: 'HDR ready' on a 250-nit panel means HDR content will look flatter than SDR.
120Hz or 144Hz matters more than resolution at this size: all five picks are 4K, so refresh rate and VRR are the real differentiators for console gaming.
Budget ₹15,000–₹25,000 for sound separately: every panel in this bracket ships with 20W–40W speakers that undersell a 65-inch picture.
meta.who_for: Anyone furnishing a living room 9 feet or deeper who wants a big-screen 4K panel that will still look modern in 2030 — mixed streaming, cricket, and PS5 or Xbox Series X gaming, without stepping up to OLED pricing.
meta.methodology: We compared 14 sixty-five-inch models listed on Amazon India, Flipkart, Reliance Digital and brand stores in September 2026 within the ₹62,000–₹80,000 band. For each panel we checked backlight technology (Mini LED vs full-array vs edge-lit), published peak brightness in nits, native refresh rate, HDR format support, HDMI 2.1 port count, audio output in watts, smart platform and update commitment, plus the warranty split between comprehensive and panel-only cover. Specifications were taken from manufacturer product pages and cross-checked against retailer listings; prices are stated as typical selling ranges because 65-inch TV pricing moves several thousand rupees during sale events.

faq.q: Is Mini LED worth the extra money over QLED at 65 inches under ₹80,000?
faq.a: Yes, if you watch in a room with any ambient light. Mini LED uses hundreds of small backlight zones that can dim independently, so bright objects stay bright while surrounding areas go dark. A QLED-labelled edge-lit panel has a handful of zones along one edge, which produces visible halos around bright objects on dark backgrounds. The Hisense E8S and TCL Q6C are the two picks here with genuine dimming-zone backlights.

faq.q: Is 65 inches too big for a small Indian living room?
faq.a: The practical rule for 4K is a viewing distance of roughly 1.2 to 1.5 times the screen diagonal, which puts a 65-inch panel at about 6.5 to 8 feet. Most Indian living rooms seat viewers 8 to 11 feet from the TV wall, so 65 inches is comfortable. Below 6 feet you will start noticing pixel structure on lower-bitrate streams and cable feeds.

faq.q: Do I need HDMI 2.1 if I only stream?
faq.a: No. Streaming apps run on the TV itself and never touch an HDMI port. HDMI 2.1 with 4K 120Hz matters for a PS5, Xbox Series X or a gaming PC. If you only use Netflix, Prime Video and JioHotstar, prioritise panel brightness and Dolby Vision support instead and treat port specs as secondary.

faq.q: Why do brand TVs cost double the unbranded 65-inch listings?
faq.a: Three reasons. First, panel grade: budget listings frequently use B-grade panels with weaker uniformity and lower brightness. Second, processing: upscaling a 1080p cable feed to 4K is a software problem, and brand processors are years ahead. Third, service: brand networks stock 65-inch replacement panels regionally, while an unbranded panel failure at month 14 often has no repair path at all.

faq.q: How long will these TVs keep receiving app updates?
faq.a: Google TV models such as the TCL Q6C and Sony K-65S30B generally get platform updates for around four years. Samsung Tizen and LG webOS keep major streaming apps working for a similar span. Custom Android builds on unbranded panels are the risk case: apps commonly stop updating within 12 to 18 months and Netflix or JioHotstar can drop certification entirely.

body:
What actually matters in a 65-inch TV under ₹80,000

Something real changed in this bracket during 2026. A year ago, ₹80,000 bought a competent 65-inch edge-lit LED panel and nothing more interesting, with Mini LED reserved for ₹1.2 lakh and up. That is no longer true: Hisense and TCL both ship genuine dimming-zone Mini LED panels at 65 inches inside this budget, so the meaningful choice is no longer which brand but which backlight technology you are actually paying for.

That matters because "QLED" has become close to meaningless as a shopping signal. QLED describes a quantum-dot colour film layered over a backlight; it says nothing about how that backlight is controlled. An edge-lit panel with a quantum-dot film is legally a QLED and will still show grey-ish blacks and visible halos.

If you only buy one thing from this list: the Hisense 65E8S. It is the cheapest 65-inch panel in India with a real Mini LED backlight, roughly 700 nits peak brightness, 144Hz with VRR for consoles, and Dolby Vision plus Dolby Atmos. Confirm the E8S suffix on the listing, because the E7 and A7 models sit at overlapping prices with materially weaker panels.

Backlight: Mini LED, full-array, or edge-lit

This is the single spec that determines how a 65-inch panel looks in a real room. Edge-lit panels put LEDs along one or two edges and diffuse light across the screen, giving perhaps two to sixteen controllable zones. Full-array panels use a grid behind the screen, typically 20 to 60 zones. Mini LED shrinks those LEDs so the same area holds hundreds of zones.

The practical difference shows up in two places. Watching a night-time cricket match, an edge-lit panel washes the stadium a uniform dark grey. On credits or subtitles over black, edge-lit panels bloom a visible glow around the text. At 65 inches both artefacts are larger and harder to ignore than on a 43-inch set.

Brightness: insist on a nits figure

Peak brightness in nits is the most commonly hidden spec in Indian TV listings, and its absence is informative. Budget 65-inch panels frequently sit at 250 to 350 nits. Mini LED models in this bracket reach roughly 600 to 700 nits. HDR content is mastered assuming displays can hit at least 600 nits, so on a 300-nit panel the HDR version of a film can genuinely look flatter than the SDR version.

Brightness also decides whether the TV is watchable in daylight. A 300-nit panel facing a window at 4pm is close to unusable; a 700-nit panel stays legible. If a listing advertises HDR without publishing a nits figure, assume it is under 350.

Refresh rate: 120Hz and 144Hz are now reachable

All five picks here are 4K, so resolution is not a differentiator at this price. Refresh rate is. A 60Hz panel is fine for films and broadcast content, which is mastered at 24 or 50 frames per second anyway. A 120Hz or 144Hz panel matters if you own a PS5, an Xbox Series X or a gaming PC, and it helps fast-panning sports look less smeary.

The related spec is VRR, or variable refresh rate, which lets the panel match the console's fluctuating output frame by frame and eliminates tearing. The Hisense E8S and TCL Q6C support both high refresh and VRR; the Sony, Samsung and LG picks are 60Hz.

Sound: assume you will add a soundbar

Every panel in this bracket ships with 20W to 40W of audio inside a chassis roughly 30mm deep, and physics does not permit meaningful bass from that enclosure. Dolby Atmos in the specification list means the TV can decode an Atmos stream, not that you will hear height channels. Plan on ₹15,000 to ₹25,000 for a 2.1 soundbar with a wireless subwoofer, and check for eARC on one HDMI port.

Warranty: read the split, not the headline

Indian TV warranties are almost always split into comprehensive cover and panel-only cover. A listing advertising a three-year warranty usually means one year comprehensive plus two years panel-only, which puts labour, mainboard, power supply and backlight driver out of scope after year one. Since backlight drivers commonly fail around year three, that split matters more than the headline number. Sony, Samsung and LG have the deepest 65-inch service coverage in tier-2 cities; Hisense and TCL remain metro-strongest.

Our top 5 picks

Top Pick

1. Hisense 65E8S Mini LED 4K Smart TV

Usually ₹72,000–₹78,000
BacklightMini LED
Refresh144Hz + VRR
HDRDolby Vision, HDR10+
OSVIDAA U

The E8S is the reason this guide exists. It is the least expensive route to a genuine Mini LED backlight at 65 inches in India, with local dimming zones that hold black properly and roughly 700 nits of peak brightness for daylight viewing and real HDR impact. It supports 144Hz with VRR, so a PS5 running a 120fps title gets the full benefit, and it decodes both Dolby Vision and HDR10+.

The compromise is the platform. VIDAA U is Hisense's own operating system rather than Google TV: all major Indian apps are present and it is responsive, but the library is smaller and third-party additions arrive later. Best for anyone who wants maximum panel quality per rupee. Confirm the E8S suffix, not E7 or A7.

What works

  • Genuine Mini LED with local dimming at this price
  • Around 700 nits peak, so HDR actually looks like HDR
  • 144Hz with VRR for current-gen consoles
  • Dolby Vision and HDR10+ both supported

Trade-offs

  • VIDAA OS has a smaller app library than Google TV
  • Service network is metro-strongest, thinner in tier-3 cities
  • Model naming is confusing; E7 and A7 sit at similar prices
  • Built-in audio still needs a soundbar

Best for Gaming

2. TCL 65Q6C QD-Mini LED Google TV

Usually ₹68,000–₹76,000
BacklightQD-Mini LED
Refresh144Hz + VRR
HDRDolby Vision
OSGoogle TV

The Q6C pairs a quantum-dot Mini LED panel with Google TV, which is the combination most buyers actually want: dimming-zone contrast plus the widest app library and Chromecast built in. It runs 144Hz with VRR and includes a game-mode overlay reporting refresh and latency on screen, useful when verifying that a console handshake negotiated 120Hz.

Against the Hisense, the Q6C typically trades slightly lower peak brightness for the better software platform and Google's four-year update cadence. Best for console-first buyers who also want a mainstream smart platform. Check whether the listing is the 144Hz variant, since regional SKUs sometimes ship 60Hz under a near-identical model code.

What works

  • Mini LED contrast with full Google TV app library
  • 144Hz with VRR and an on-screen game-mode readout
  • Chromecast built in, no dongle needed
  • Roughly four years of platform updates

Trade-offs

  • Peak brightness typically below the Hisense E8S
  • Regional SKUs vary; 60Hz variants exist under similar codes
  • Stock remote is plasticky for the price
  • Google TV home screen is ad-heavy by default
Check current price
Best Processing

3. Sony Bravia 65 K-65S30B 4K Google TV

Usually ₹74,000–₹80,000
BacklightDirect LED
Refresh60Hz
HDRDolby Vision, HDR10
OSGoogle TV

Sony's argument in 2026 is not panel specification, it is processing. The K-65S30B uses a direct-lit LED panel rather than Mini LED, so on paper it loses to the Hisense and TCL. In practice, Sony's X1 processor handles the thing Indian households do most: upscaling 1080p and sub-1080p sources. Cable feeds and older catalogue titles look noticeably cleaner here than on either Mini LED pick.

It is 60Hz, so console gamers should look elsewhere. Best for a household whose viewing is mostly broadcast cricket, cable and mixed-quality streaming. Verify the model code, since the older K-65X75K still sells at a lower price and is a different panel.

What works

  • Best upscaling of low-bitrate cable and streaming content
  • Google TV with a long update commitment
  • Widest service network of any brand here
  • Motion handling on sports is class-leading at 60Hz

Trade-offs

  • Direct LED, not Mini LED, so weaker black-level control
  • 60Hz only, no benefit from a PS5 at 120fps
  • Most expensive pick in this list
  • Older X75K variant muddies the shopping process
Check current price
Best Value

4. Samsung 65 Crystal 4K UA65DUE70B

Usually ₹62,000–₹70,000
BacklightEdge LED
Refresh60Hz
HDRHDR10+
OSTizen

This is the cheapest way into a 65-inch panel from a brand with nationwide service, which is a legitimate reason to buy it. Tizen is the fastest-feeling smart platform here, the remote is the best of the five, and Samsung's service network reaches genuinely small towns. The panel is edge-lit and supports HDR10+ but not Dolby Vision.

Missing Dolby Vision matters more than it used to, because Netflix and JioHotstar both lean on it; you still get HDR10 fallback without scene-by-scene metadata. Best for a bright room where black-level performance is less visible anyway.

What works

  • Lowest entry price for a 65-inch brand panel
  • Tizen is fast and clean, best remote in this group
  • Deepest small-town service coverage
  • Solid SDR colour accuracy out of the box

Trade-offs

  • Edge-lit backlight, visible blooming on dark scenes
  • No Dolby Vision, HDR10+ only
  • 60Hz, and 20W audio is weak for the screen size
  • Peak brightness well below the Mini LED picks
Check current price
Best Interface

5. LG 65UT80 4K UHD Smart TV

Usually ₹66,000–₹73,000
BacklightDirect LED
Refresh60Hz
HDRHDR10
OSwebOS

The UT80 is the pick for anyone who has to share a remote with people who dislike smart TVs. webOS with the Magic Remote pointer is the most approachable interface in this category by a wide margin: you point at the screen and click, no D-pad navigation required. The panel is direct-lit with better uniformity than the Samsung.

It is 60Hz and HDR10 only, with no Dolby Vision. Best for a mixed-age household where interface friction is the real problem. Confirm the panel variant, since LG's UT and UR series overlap heavily in price.

What works

  • Magic Remote pointer is the easiest interface for non-technical users
  • Direct-lit panel with good uniformity
  • Neutral, accurate SDR colour without calibration
  • Strong service network across metros and tier-2

Trade-offs

  • HDR10 only, no Dolby Vision
  • 60Hz, so no console high-refresh benefit
  • webOS app library trails Google TV
  • UT and UR series naming overlap is confusing

The one we recommend skipping

Skip This

Unbranded 65-inch "QLED" listings

Usually ₹38,000–₹52,000
BacklightEdge LED
Refresh60Hz
HDRHDR10 claimed
OSCustom Android

Every sale event fills the 65-inch category with listings from brands you have not heard of, priced ₹20,000 to ₹35,000 below the picks above and carrying a QLED badge. The badge is technically accurate and practically meaningless: it confirms a quantum-dot film, not a controlled backlight. These are edge-lit panels, typically 250 to 300 nits, usually with no published nits figure at all.

Three failure modes make these a bad purchase rather than a compromise. The smart platform is custom Android rather than certified Google TV, so app support commonly degrades within 12 to 18 months and Netflix or JioHotstar can lose certification entirely. Upscaling is poor, so the cable feed that makes up most real viewing looks soft at this size. And decisively, service: when one fails at month 14, there is frequently no regional partner holding a replacement 65-inch panel.

If ₹62,000 is genuinely out of reach, buy a 55-inch panel from a brand with service coverage instead. The extra ten inches are not worth an unrepairable display.

What works

  • Genuinely large screen for the money
  • 4K resolution on the specification sheet
  • Often bundled with wall mount and installation

Trade-offs

  • Edge-lit, low brightness, no published nits figure
  • Custom Android loses app certification within 12–18 months
  • Weak upscaling, and cable feeds look poor at this size
  • No reliable 65-inch panel service path after failure

The bottom line

The headline change in this bracket is that Mini LED is no longer a premium-only technology at 65 inches. Accept a smaller app library in exchange.

For that panel technology with mainstream software, the TCL 65Q6C is the same idea on Google TV. If most of your viewing is cable and mixed-quality streaming, the Sony K-65S30B wins on processing despite the weaker backlight. On a tight budget the Samsung UA65DUE70B has the best service reach here, and the LG 65UT80 is the pick when ease of use outranks specification.
